title: National and subnational short-term forecasting of COVID-19 in Germany and Poland during early 2021
contribution: Second and final part of the pre-registered German and Polish COVID-19 Forecast Hub evaluation (Jan-Apr 2021): 15 models from 14 teams scored by WIS against naive baselines, with quantile ensembles performing best; Bertsimas's DELPHI team contributed one model, which was worse than the naive baseline in 9 of 16 national cells.
problem_entry: {AP; no optimization model} Forecasts that inform public-health decisions need prospective, pre-registered evaluation to prevent selective reporting and hindsight bias. This is the second part of a study pre-registered on 8 Oct 2020, covering forecasts made 11 Jan-29 Mar 2021 (p. 2). Bertsimas enters only as a member of the contributing CovidAnalytics-DELPHI team (p. 23).
key_idea: One submission format for real-time quantile forecasts (15 models, 14 teams). Forecasts are scored on the weighted interval score against three pre-specified naive baselines and combined into median (primary), mean and inverse-WIS quantile ensembles (pp. 4-6).
assumptions: Truth data: RKI and Polish Ministry of Health (primary) or JHU. A point forecast plus 23 quantiles per weekly target, at horizons of 1-4 weeks with the focus on 1-2. Missing weeks are imputed with the worst score of any model. DELPHI is listed as a compartmental model on JHU truth data (pp. 3-5).
proof_devices: n/a for his contribution; the paper's own device is the WIS definition and its decomposition into spread, over- and underprediction (pp. 4-5)
quantile-averaging (Vincentization) ensembles with heuristic, not estimated, inverse-WIS weights (p. 6)
experiments: 12 weekly forecasts per target, national plus 16 German states and 16 Polish voivodeships (Tables 2-3, pp. 12-13). The median ensemble was among the best (p. 9). DELPHI's relative WIS against the last-value baseline was above 1 in 9 of 16 national cells: Germany 1-wk cases 1.04 and 1-wk deaths 1.77; Poland cases 1.33-1.54 and deaths 1.46, 1.08 and 1.09. It was below 1 for German cases and deaths at 2-4 weeks (down to 0.43) and for Polish 3-wk deaths, 0.97 (Table S1, p. 39). Several DELPHI entries include imputed worst weeks (Table 2, p. 12).
positioning: Builds on the US COVID-19 Forecast Hub and the collaborative hub concept (FluSight, DARPA Chikungunya Challenge, Dengue Forecasting Project). The platform merged into the ECDC European hub in April 2021 (pp. 2, 18).
writing: Pre-registration is foregrounded. The team count is stated inconsistently: 'fifteen independent modelling teams' (p. 2) against fifteen models from fourteen teams (p. 5). The contribution statement separates the writers (JB, TG, MSe) from the forecast contributors (pp. 22-23).
limits_future: Turning points and the forecaster's dilemma (p. 17), the choice of baseline (p. 16), heuristic ensemble weights (p. 17) and changing case ascertainment (p. 17). Next: hospitalization forecasts in the European hub (p. 18).

method_links.note: DELPHI is judged on predictions, on the field's metric (WIS) against naive rules, not on decisions. Most cells are worse than the naive baseline, some with imputed weeks. This second hub supports Method 5's critic-informed checkpoint ('score forecasts on the field's metric'). Heuristic 4 evidence: his team submitted to a pre-registered, prospective external scoreboard.

transferable: Pre-register targets, horizons, baselines and the rule for missing forecasts before any forecast is scored (pp. 2, 5).
Impute a missing forecast week with the worst score any model achieved that week, so selective submission cannot help (p. 5).

Report scores relative to several pre-specified naive baselines (last value carried forward, trend extrapolation, exponential smoothing), because any one baseline may suit one period by luck (pp. 5-6, 16).
Decompose WIS into spread, over- and underprediction to tell a team which way to fix its intervals (pp. 4-5, 9).
coauthors: 42 authors; the manuscript was written by J. Bracher, T. Gneiting and M. Schienle (KIT/HITS). His DELPHI teammates were Michael Lingzhi Li (MIT ORC; his PhD student, PhD 2022 per 04-mentorship.md) and Saksham Soni (MIT Sloan) (pp. 1, 23).

quotes.text: JB, TG and MSe wrote the manuscript.
The pre-specified median ensemble was consistently among the best-performing methods

title: Tabtext: A flexible and contextual approach to tabular data representation
contribution: TabText turns tabular health records into paragraphs embedded by a fine-tuned clinical language model. The task-agnostic features train accurate patient-flow models across six hospitals with minimal preprocessing and add up to about 4 AUC points on hard or low-data tasks (text read: arXiv v5, 2025, retitled).
problem_entry: {ML AP; no optimization model} Tabular health data need heavy manual cleaning and lose their context. Prior language-based approaches embed each data stream separately inside task-specific networks; none shows task-agnostic embeddings, a study of augmentation or cross-institution performance (p. 2).
key_idea: Each patient-day becomes a paragraph ('attribute is value'; numbers binned to words; missing values omitted; table metadata added). A masked-LM fine-tuned Clinical-Longformer embeds it (768-d mean pooling), and any standard model uses the embedding, alone or concatenated with tabular features (pp. 2-5).
assumptions: Design choices were fixed on a 2017 development set of hospital HA: 60,000 + 10,000 patient-days, 63 lab columns, nine patient-flow targets (p. 3). Evaluation: HA from Jan 2018 to Apr 2022 (160 columns) and five more hospitals of the same system with non-standardized records (pp. 5-6), plus nine UCI datasets (p. 8).
proof_devices: n/a (no formal analysis). Design choices were selected by statistical comparison: the LLM (p. 4), the median rank of 16 sentence configurations (p. 5), and fine-tuning, significant (p < 0.0001) on 8 of 9 tasks (p. 5).
experiments: Temporal split (train 2018-Feb 2020, validate Mar-Dec 2020, test Jan 2021-Apr 2022) on HA and five other hospitals: AUC 0.694-0.941 (Table 1, p. 6). Augmentation adds 1-3 points when the baseline AUC is at most 0.80 and training is at most 10k, and is negligible or slightly negative for short-horizon mortality (Fig. 3, pp. 7-8). UCI: FT-Transformer, LR and XGBoost over 10 splits; breast cancer +0.039, HD -0.010 (Table 2, pp. 8-9). Code is released for the public datasets (p. 10).
positioning: Follows three lines of language-based work on structured health data: domain foundation models, EHR-sequence models, and table-to-text embeddings with extra architectures. It claims none had task-agnostic embeddings, augmentation or cross-institution evidence (pp. 2, 9).
writing: v5 has a Lancet-style structured abstract (Background, Methods, Findings, Interpretation, Funding) (p. 1) and a specific limitations paragraph (p. 9). The contribution statement assigns DB to inspiring, supporting, supervising and editing (p. 10). The abstract's 'tested prospectively' denotes a temporal hold-out (pp. 1, 6).
limits_future: Embedding overhead; embeddings less interpretable than raw features; one health system; data errors carried into representations; subgroup performance unstudied (p. 9). The hospital data are not shareable (p. 10).

method_links.note: The evaluation is deployment-like (temporal and cross-hospital) but scores predictions (AUC) only, with no decision metric and no hospital rule as a baseline; the decision use sits in the companion operations paper (ref. [14]). Heuristic 4 evidence: the null and negative cells are printed (HD -1 point; short-horizon mortality). Tension with Taste mark 5: the embeddings are less interpretable (p. 9).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Variant: trained at one hospital (HA, 2018-2020) and tested at HA and five other hospitals of the same system over Jan 2021-Apr 2022, with non-standardized records. Same name as c41 S679 and S680.

transferable: Fix every design choice (language model, text template, fine-tuning) on a separate development year before the evaluation years are touched (pp. 3-5).
Choose among template variants by median rank across all tasks, not by one task's score (Fig. 2b, p. 5).
Use a temporal train/validation/test split plus other sites of the same system to mimic deployment, and say that it is a hold-out, not a prospective trial (p. 6).

coauthors: Kimberly Villalobos Carballo (first author; his PhD student, thesis 2024 per 04-mentorship.md), Liangyuan Na, Yu Ma, Leonard Boussioux, Cynthia Zeng and Luis Soenksen; Bertsimas is last author (p. 1).

title: The backbone method for ultra-high dimensional sparse machine learning
contribution: The backbone method scales exact sparse learning. It solves many small feature-subset subproblems, takes the union of their supports, and solves the exact MIO only on that backbone: sparse regression to 10^7-10^8 features and trees to 10^5, with a high-probability support-recovery theorem for a simplified version.
problem_entry: {ML IO} Exact MIO methods stop at p ~ 10^5 (sparse regression) and p ~ 10^3 (trees). Screening is heuristic and suboptimal, and feature extraction is uninterpretable (pp. 2-3). Ultra-high dimensional is defined as p > n and two orders of magnitude beyond the exact method's limit (p. 2). The device was inspired by large-scale online vehicle routing (p. 3).
key_idea: The backbone is the union of supports from many tractable subproblems, built hierarchically until |B| <= Bmax: an SIS screen keeping alpha*p ~ 10n features, utility-weighted feature sampling, and fast sparse fits by the subgradient method, elastic net or CART. The exact MIO (cutting planes or OCT) is then solved on B (pp. 9-20). It is the union of near-optimal solutions, unlike SAT's intersection of optimal ones (pp. 7-8).
assumptions: Sparse ERM with a ridge term and ||w||_0 <= k, k known (pp. 4, 15); depth-D trees with minbucket (p. 19). The theory assumes a Gaussian design, beta in {-1,0,1}^p, Gaussian noise, log p = O(n^xi) and gamma = 1/n, for a one-round uniform-sampling simplification that the authors call 'very simple and rather unrealistic' (pp. 18, 40-41).
proof_devices: Theorem 1: alpha = Theta(n^(1-phi)/p) and M = Omega(log(alpha p k)/log(1/(1-beta+beta p_sub))) give a vanishing probability of missing a relevant feature (pp. 18-19)
a union bound over the screening failure (Fan-Lv SIS theorem) and the per-feature misses (pp. 41-42)
relevant features absent from a subproblem are treated as extra Gaussian noise, so the Bertsimas-Van Parys support-recovery theorem applies (Lemma 1, p. 43)
a binomial count of the subproblems containing a feature plus the binomial theorem: k(1-beta+beta p_sub)^M (p. 44)
complexity O(np + M alpha beta p log(alpha p) + M (alpha beta p)^2 n) with LARS subproblems, and an iteration bound from halving M (pp. 14-15)
experiments: Setup: Xeon E5-2690, CentOS 7, Gurobi (version not given), and the commercial Interpretable AI package for SR-REL and OCT (pp. 23-24). Synthetic regression reaches 3x10^8 features in under 10 h and trees reach 10^5 (p. 25), against SIS-ENET, CART and exact SR/OCT on the full set (pp. 25-30). Four UCI sets, each with 1,000 permuted copies per feature, 25 runs (pp. 36-37). Losses are printed: housing R2 0.765 against SIS-ENET's 0.863 (p. 38); a slight OCT edge at p = 2,000 (pp. 29-30); higher RF AUC (p. 39). Parameters were not tuned (p. 24).
positioning: Set against screening (SIS), feature extraction and distributed methods (DECO, ADMM); Hazimeh et al.'s solver is named as compatible. It distinguishes its backbone from the SAT backbone and traces it to the group's 2019 online taxi-routing paper (pp. 4-8).
writing: Contributions are bullets with headline scales (p. 8). The theory is framed as hyperparameter guidance, with the model admitted to be unrealistic (p. 18). Certificates are scoped 'albeit for the reduced problem' (p. 8), and each optimality gap is tied to the formulation it refers to (p. 23).
limits_future: k assumed known (p. 4); idealized theory for a simplified algorithm (pp. 18, 41); no tuning (p. 24); tree sensitivity analysis omitted (p. 30). Next: sparse SVMs, sparse PCA, clustering, distributed implementation (p. 40).

method_links.note: The exact MIO formulation stays the target; the backbone only shrinks the instance until the class's own solver (cutting planes, OCT) applies.

Evidence: warm starts (incremental cross-validation, subgradient), a 5-minute limit per gamma, gaps printed but scoped to the reduced problem, and duels with SIS-ENET, RFE, DECO, CART, RF and oracles. Variant: OCT is a tailored local search run through the commercial Interpretable AI package, so the tree results carry no certificate. Heuristic 3 variant: when the exact model stalls at scale, the paper shrinks the instance rather than running local search on the whole problem.
The 'why now' is a single sentence ('far beyond what one would imagine a decade ago') with no rebuilt solver x hardware figure; the scale limits come from the group's own papers.
Weak: the group's company software (Interpretable AI) is the experimental platform for SR-REL and OCT.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: shrink-then-solve with a printed quality/time knob
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The backbone is built, then the exact problem is solved on it. The screening fraction alpha trades time against accuracy ('There is a trade-off between the two'), and beta ~ 0.5 and Bmax are studied. Same name as c11 S160 and S073; compare S443 in this batch.
Variant (a device, not a lemma): the backbone moves from the group's online vehicle-routing work {AP} to sparse ML {ML}. Compare c07 S019.

transferable: Scale an exact sparse model with a union-of-supports backbone. Screen first, sample feature subsets with probability rising in marginal utility, fit a fast sparse heuristic to each subset, take the union, halve the number of subproblems per round until |B| <= Bmax, then solve exactly on B (pp. 9-15).
Set the number of subproblems from a union bound plus a binomial count, P(miss j) <= (1-beta+beta p_sub)^M (pp. 43-44), and use that M in the experiments (p. 34).
To reuse a full-problem recovery theorem inside a subproblem, treat the relevant features left out of the subproblem as added Gaussian noise (Lemma 1, p. 43).
Test support recovery on real data by appending 1,000 random permutations of each feature and counting how many selected features are originals, over 5 splits x 5 expansions (pp. 36-37).
Name the formulation a reported optimality gap belongs to, original or reduced problem (p. 23).
coauthors: Vassilis Digalakis Jr. (MIT ORC; his PhD student, thesis 2023 per 04-mentorship.md)

quotes.text: The model we examine is indeed very simple and rather unrealistic
while providing optimality guarantees, albeit for the reduced problem

title: Distributionally robust causal inference with observational data
contribution: Bounds average treatment effects under unobserved confounding by distributionally robust optimization over counterfactual distributions. It shows that the marginal sensitivity model is a special case and proposes a distributional sensitivity model (shape match up to a location shift) that stays informative under strong confounding, with DiD, IV and high-dimensional extensions.
problem_entry: {RO ML} Unconfoundedness often lacks credibility, and Tan's marginal sensitivity model gives uninformative bounds when unobserved confounders strongly affect treatment and outcome. The entry is to state the departure as an ambiguity set and bound the ATT by DRO (pp. 1-2, 5-7).
key_idea: Minimize the ATT over counterfactual distributions written as bounded reweightings of observed control outcomes; Proposition 1 recovers the MSM. The DSM adds that the counterfactual matches the treated group's outcome distribution up to a location shift within KS distance delta, and it allows zero weights (lack of overlap). It is solved as a MILO by discretizing the shift (pp. 5-10).
assumptions: IID units, no interference, nonparametric outcome and treatment models; categorical covariates first (p. 4). The DSM is credible when treatment-effect heterogeneity is small relative to outcome variation; Proposition 2 assumes minimally k-Lipschitz CDFs (pp. 7-9). Knobs: Gamma, delta and epsilon (pp. 8, 11, 13). IV assumes monotonicity and a relaxed exclusion restriction (pp. 12-14).
proof_devices: Proposition 1: the MSM is equivalent to a DRO problem over a weighting ambiguity set (p. 7; proof p. 26)
Proposition 2: shift-KS distance <= 3(k sigma01/2)^(2/3), via Lipschitz continuity plus Chebyshev, optimizing the split point (pp. 8-9; proof p. 27)
Theorem 1: bounds on sampling weights are equivalent to a distance bound, a quasimetric for Gamma < 2 and a metric for Gamma >= 2 (pp. 9-10)
MILO reformulation: bound the shift by the outcome range, discretize it, and choose one grid point with binaries (p. 10)
experiments: Simulation: 3 scenarios, n in {100, 200, 500}, 1,000 runs. The DSM is less conservative than the MSM, with the gap growing in Gamma; its s.d. is larger than the MSM's in every cell, which is not discussed (Table 1, pp. 15-17). NSW with PSID/CPS controls: smaller bias than LaLonde's regression against the $886 benchmark (Tables 2-3, pp. 18-19). BMC diabetes against Causal Forests and a doubly robust estimator, argued by plausibility (p. 20). STAR: the estimate turns negative as Gamma grows (p. 21). Gurobi is named without a version, and no solve times are given (p. 10).
positioning: Set against Rosenbaum-style and regression-based sensitivity analyses and against partial identification. It joins robust optimization for causal inference (mostly policy learning) and cites Bertsimas and den Hertog (2022) for DRO (pp. 2-3).
writing: The related-work paragraph ends mid-sentence ('exploits the commonly used assumption that', p. 3). 'Distributional KL distance' is used where the model uses the KS distance (pp. 18, 20). The conclusion has two sentences (pp. 21-22).
limits_future: Small samples make the DSM overly conservative (p. 21). No next step is stated (pp. 21-22). Not discussed: the DSM's larger variance (p. 16) and solve times (p. 10).

method_links.note: Sensitivity analysis, a problem owned by statistics, is written as DRO; the incumbent is recovered exactly and the new model is kept in the MILO class. Heuristic 1 evidence: a procedure practice already uses (Tan's MSM) is the exact robust problem over one ambiguity set, which is then extended.

Interpretable knobs: Gamma is set by the minimum number of units kept (25/12/8 for 30/60/100), and delta is tied to effect heterogeneity by Proposition 2. Estimates are tabulated by knob and the bad case is printed (STAR), but there is no single price curve and no solution-independent violation bound.
Scored by bias against experimental benchmarks, not by decisions. The BMC clinical reading rests on plausibility (an HbA1c change of >= 1.5 points is 'highly unlikely'), not on a scored decision.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Proposition 1: Tan's marginal sensitivity model is the DRO problem over a weighting ambiguity set. Same name as c04, c10, c20, c31, c32 and s01.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: exact dictionary between a statistical procedure and a robust model, with its boundary
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The MSM equals DRO over a weighting set, and its boundary is printed: non-informative under strong confounding. Theorem 1 adds a weights <-> metric dictionary. Same name as c19 S039, S085 and S104.

transferable: Turn a sensitivity model into DRO: write the unobserved counterfactual distribution as a bounded reweighting of an observed one, minimize the effect over that set, and recover the incumbent model as one choice of set (pp. 6-7).

Borrow shape information from the other arm: require the counterfactual to match the treated outcomes up to a location shift, and make delta interpretable by bounding it with effect heterogeneity (Lipschitz plus Chebyshev, optimized over the split) (pp. 8-9, 27).
Make a minimum-over-shifts KS constraint MILO-solvable: bound the shift by the outcome range, discretize it, and select a grid point with binaries (p. 10).
Choose the weight bound Gamma by the minimum effective sample it implies, not as an abstract odds ratio (pp. 18-20).
Validate an observational estimator where an experimental answer exists: LaLonde's NSW with non-experimental controls, and STAR with school-permuted controls (Wilde-Hollister) (pp. 17-21).
coauthors: Kosuke Imai (Harvard, Government and Statistics); Michael Lingzhi Li (Harvard Business School; his former PhD student, PhD 2022 per 04-mentorship.md)

This suggests that with a small sample size, the distributional sensitivity model may yield an overly conservative estimate.

title: Sparse PCA: A geometric approach
contribution: GeoSPCA builds all orthogonal sparse principal components with a common support of size k at once. A left-eigenvector reformulation is approximated as a binary linear problem with lazy no-good cuts, with tight gap bounds and finite convergence; it solves instances with p in the 10,000s in at most 2 minutes.
problem_entry: {ML IO} Cardinality-controlled sparse PCA builds PCs one by one by deflation, losing overall optimality and orthogonality, and penalty methods cannot fix k. Only Del Pia (2022, theory) and Dey et al. (2022, p up to 2,000) build several PCs at once (pp. 2-4).
key_idea: In the left-eigenvector form, the support choice is picking the k columns with the largest projected norms (Prop. 1). The nonconcave objective is replaced by the sum of column norms plus the condition that the chosen submatrix is within eta of rank a. That condition is enforced by lazily generated no-good cuts, each separated by one n x k SVD, and Algorithm 2 lowers eta while keeping the best support (pp. 6-15).
assumptions: Centered X; a orthonormal PCs sharing one support of size <= k (p. 6). The low-rank-plus-noise picture is intuition only, 'not a required assumption in any of the results' (p. 11). Lemma 9 assumes a unique optimum of (7) (p. 14). a is chosen by the PCA elbow and eta by Algorithm 2 (p. 22).
proof_devices: Proposition 1: equivalence with a left-eigenvector support problem (pp. 6-7)
Theorem 4: an eta interval exists in which the surrogate's optima are true optima (p. 10)
Proposition 5: surrogate loss <= eta, tight on a 2 x 4 example (pp. 11-12)
Proposition 6 and Corollaries 7-8: an a priori bound from the classical-PCA residual (pp. 12-13)
Proposition 10: finite convergence of Algorithm 2; Proposition 11: the cut history gives an upper bound and an optimality test (pp. 15-16)
an explicit instance (k = 2, a = 1) that forces exponentially many cuts; per-iteration cost O(k^3 + nk^2) (pp. 16-17)
experiments: Laptop i7-8750H, Gurobi 9.1, Python 3.6.5 (p. 22). Mturk, Colon, Arcene and CGD (p up to 22,283, k up to 270), against greedy and PathSPCA with Schur deflation: up to +24.2% over greedy, with one loss (Colon, k = 33, -0.3%) and gap bounds of 0-23%. GeoSPCA takes at most 118 s, against minutes to 51 h for the baselines on the two large sets (Tables 1-2, pp. 25-26). AR face recognition against SSPCA and PCA (Fig. 9, p. 30). No comparison with Dey et al. (2022).
positioning: Draws a two-category map of sparse PCA (penalized approximation vs cardinality-controlled) and criticizes deflation. Notes that Del Pia's result is theoretical only and that Dey et al. reach p = 2,000. Places the group's own branch-and-bound/SDO work among the deflation methods (pp. 2-4).
writing: The abstract's headline 'up to 24%' is the best single instance (p. 25). Small gains are motivated as 'more lives saved or increased profits' (p. 24). The BLO is kept partly to make a point that solving can be competitive (p. 17). There are several typos (pp. 22-23).
limits_future: Potentially exponential number of cuts (p. 16); polyhedral pattern formulations are beyond scope (p. 29). Next: more efficient cuts and more sparse PCA variants (p. 31).

method_links.note: A nonconvex problem owned by the deflation and penalty schools is rewritten as a binary linear problem with lazy cuts; the tractability boundary is printed as an exponential-cut instance.

Each instance carries a gap bound or an optimality proof (Props. 5, 11); the method duels the greedy incumbent and deflation, and a loss is printed. One joint model replaces sequential deflation (Taste mark 3). Partial: no warm start and no stated time limit. Heuristic 9: the abstract's 'up to 24%' is the best instance; most gains are 0.4-5%.
The intractability belief is challenged in words (the BLO is kept 'to illustrate' that solving can be competitive), without a speed-up figure.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Variant: the reformulation explains why the incumbent greedy works, because columns with large norms dominate the objective. Same name as c04 S025/S015 and s01 S229.

transferable: Write cardinality-constrained PCA in the left-eigenvector space, where the support choice becomes selecting the k columns with the largest projected norms (pp. 6-7).
Replace an intractable objective by a linear surrogate plus a feasibility test that a small linear-algebra routine (one SVD) can separate, and add no-good cuts lazily (pp. 8-10, 13-14).
Prove that the surrogate loses at most the slack parameter, show tightness on a tiny example, and give an a priori version from a classical solution (pp. 11-13).
Turn the history of generated cuts into an upper bound and an optimality test for the incumbent (p. 16).
Construct and print the instance on which your own cut loop is exponential (p. 16).
coauthors: Driss Lahlou Kitane (MIT ORC; his student per 04-mentorship.md)

quotes.text: too often, solving is deemed computationally costly while in practice it can be competitive
Formulation (2) sheds a light on one reason the greedy approach performs well.

title: Stochastic cutting planes for data-driven optimization
contribution: Stochastic cutting planes build each outer-approximation cut from a fresh random subset of the data. They terminate finitely with an epsilon-optimal solution, with exponentially vanishing failure probability, and speed up sparse regression, SVM and SAA knapsack problems by one to two orders of magnitude (text read: arXiv v1).
problem_entry: {IO ML; DA via SAA} Outer approximation needs f and its gradient on all N samples for every cut, which blocks N >= 10^6, while the MILO master is cheap (pp. 2, 9). The entry transplants the SGD idea into an exact discrete method, which the authors 'could not find' studied (p. 2). It is distinct from randomized constraint generation (pp. 3-4).
key_idea: Each cut is built from n << N samples drawn afresh without replacement; the master MILO and the termination test are unchanged. The default is n = min{N, 10 sqrt(N)} (Algorithm 2, pp. 10, 12).
assumptions: Convex, once-differentiable f and g; finite Z and compact Theta; concentration of f and its gradient on random subsets at rate sqrt(log(1/eps)/n), without unbiasedness (p. 5). Separable losses qualify by Hoeffding without replacement (Lemma 1, p. 7), and non-separable sparse ridge regression by Lemma 2 (p. 8). Nonconvex problems can be run without guarantees (p. 5).
proof_devices: Theorem 1: finite termination w.p. 1 with E[K] <= (e-1)|Z| + 1, and epsilon-optimality w.p. >= 1 - (2K+1) exp(-n eps^2/((2+sqrt(p1+p2))^2 J)) (pp. 10-11)

termination: a repeated integer point must show strictly increasing sampled values; exchangeability gives probability <= 1/q! for an increasing run, plus pigeonhole over |Z|(q-1)+1 iterations (pp. 26-27)
feasibility is inherited from Fletcher-Leyffer (p. 27); optimality via Lemmas 5-6: Frechet's inequality, per-cut concentration and convexity (pp. 28-29)
Lemma 2 via the Woodbury identity and finite-population Hoeffding (pp. 21-22)
experiments: Julia 1.4.2 on a six-core i7-5820k with 24 GB. Sparse regression, N to 10^6: 1,356 s against 46 s, with identical MAPE (Table 1, p. 12). SVM on covertype, N to 10^5, against LIBSVM and scikit-learn SGD: 13x and 30x faster for about 0.5% accuracy, but a 2.6-point drop at N = 10^3 that is not discussed (Table 2, p. 14). SSKP SAA with Gurobi 9.0.1: two orders faster, and the linear reformulation fails at N = 10^6 (Table 3, p. 16). The (N, n) grids put the needed n between O(log N) and O(sqrt N) (Figs. 1-2, pp. 17-18).
positioning: Extends Duran-Grossmann and Fletcher-Leyffer outer approximation. Distinguishes itself from Parikh's approximate cuts and from randomized constraint generation (Volkov-Zavriev, Calafiore-Campi), and complements SAA (Kleywegt et al.). It generalizes Bertsimas-Li 2018, which needed strong convexity (pp. 3-4).
writing: The SGD analogy is the framing (p. 2), and novelty is claimed by absence ('could not find any detailed work', p. 2). The pseudo-code comment '# Return the filled matrix X' is apparently left over from the matrix-completion paper (pp. 9-10). There are typos in Theorem 1 (data d1..dn) and in reformulation (10) (zj for xj) (pp. 10, 16). The conclusion is one paragraph (p. 19).
limits_future: No guarantee without convexity (p. 5); worst-case E[K] exponential in p1, defended by p1 << n << N (p. 11); the conclusion names no limits or next steps (p. 19). Not discussed: sampled cuts need not under-estimate the full objective, so the final bound certifies nothing (pp. 10-11).

method_links.note: The heuristic warm start and the duels with the standard cutting plane, LIBSVM, SGD and the Gurobi linear reformulation are present. But the certificate becomes a high-probability epsilon-optimality statement, and the loss of a valid lower bound is not mentioned.
Weak: the problems stay convex MINLO with a MILO master. On the SSKP the device (cuts on the [.]+ cost), not the solver, decides tractability: the N-auxiliary-variable linear reformulation fails.
MILO progress (Bixby-Rothberg; Achterberg-Wunderling) is cited to move the bottleneck to cut generation, not to reopen an intractable problem; no figure is rebuilt.

The sample size n is the one knob: Theorem 1 bounds failure in n, and measured agreement curves are handed to the practitioner. The property priced is speed, and the bad cells (below 100% agreement on the 10 log N line) appear only in the figure.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: carry deterministic devices into the stochastic version and measure what survives
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Variant: an exact algorithm, not a model, is randomized. Finite termination survives within a factor (e-1) of the deterministic |Z|; optimality survives only with high probability. Same name as c01 and s01.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: shrink-then-solve with a printed quality/time knob
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Variant: the shrinking is per cut. Each cut sees n << N samples, and Figs. 1-2 print agreement and optimality against n. Same name as c11; compare S300 in this batch.

transferable: Before speeding up an exact method, profile it: show that the master solve is cheap and that oracle work (cut generation) dominates, then attack only that part (p. 9).

State the sampling assumption as concentration of the subsampled objective and gradient, not unbiasedness, so that non-separable objectives can qualify (Woodbury plus finite-population Hoeffding) (pp. 5, 8, 21-22).

Prove finite termination of a randomized cutting-plane loop over a finite set by exchangeability: an increasing run of q i.i.d. sampled values has probability <= 1/q!, so E[K] <= (e-1)|Z| + 1 (pp. 26-27).
Print a phase diagram over (N, n) with reference curves 10 sqrt(N), 10 N^(1/3) and 10 log N, showing where the sampled method agrees with the exact one (Figs. 1-2, pp. 17-18).
Show that the gain comes from fresh randomness, not from size alone: the sampled method beats the full method run on a fixed sample of comparable size (p. 14).
